toc.title: Step one: write down the five domains

blocks.p: I want to help you practice validation. A lot of my clients and community members struggle with it.

Validation is basically recognizing what is true: acknowledging how you feel, what you're thinking, or what sensations you have inside. That's difficult for people to do, to recognize what's happening within them and be honest with themselves. Instead, we default to minimizing, or excusing, or denial, and other cognitive skills we have.

So we're going to practice, but we're not going to make it personal. We're going to make it more objective. I'll share a short story, written by ChatGPT, my helper, and we'll try to validate some of the experiences Maria is having in it.

blocks.h: Step one: write down the five domains

blocks.p: Get out something to write on, and write down these five domains:
Here's what each one means.

ul: Impulses are what the body wants to do, or has a natural reflex to do. In the flight state, the impulse might be to run away. In the fight state, there could be an impulse to push, or strangle, or pull, or lift.
Sensations are the bodily experience of an emotion. If you have an emotion of sadness, the sensations might be things like heaviness or emptiness.
Cognitions are the things in our brain: not just words, but also images and memories and calculations, all the stuff our brain does.
Emotions are, well, sad and happy and relaxed and scared. Those emotions.

blocks.p: The domains work as a cross reference. If you know your emotion, you can use it to identify what sensations might be connected to it, as well as what cognitions, impulses, and Polyvagal state.
As you read, pause whenever you need to, and write down what you notice in each of the five domains. Then I'll share what I see.

q: Maria had just finished a long day of work and was finally sitting down to relax. She scrolled through her phone, noticing that a few of her friends had made plans without her. A wave of discomfort washed over her. Her chest tightened, her stomach churned, and a thought flashed: "They must not like me as much anymore." Her heart started to race, and she could feel a heaviness in her limbs. She stared at her phone, tempted to message one of them, to ask why she hadn't been invited. But she hesitated, unsure if it could make things worse. A part of her wanted to pull away entirely, to shut off her phone and retreat into her room. Another part of her felt the urge to react, to demand an explanation. She let out a long breath, unsure of what to do next, feeling the loneliness and rejection settling deeper.

blocks.p: Hopefully you've already paused and filled in some of these. Let's go through what I noticed, starting with emotions.
What I heard was sadness, rejection, and maybe anxiety. Her heart's starting to race. That could be some anxiety. It also could be fear.

You'll notice that none of this is really hard and concrete. It's open for debate which emotions were there. Some are pretty clear, I think. Rejection is pretty darn clear: she wasn't invited, and so she felt rejected. Another one the story doesn't flat out say is that she could have felt anger. One thing she felt the impulse to do was demand an explanation, which sounds like it could have some anger in it.

Next, thoughts. I tend to group cognitions and emotions together as the top level, maybe tertiary, the third level of our experiences. Behaviors might be a fourth level after that. Cognitions and emotions really reinforce each other, and we can get stuck in cognitions and/or emotions. Our thoughts definitely feed into our emotions, and our emotions definitely feed into our thoughts. That's why we're focusing on them first. I think they're typically more accessible, at least consciously.
So what thoughts can we validate? What thoughts can we acknowledge are real for her, are true? One was really obvious: "They must not like me as much anymore."
Another one may not be so obvious. She wanted to ask why she hadn't been invited, so she had the cognition of asking a question: "Why wasn't I invited?" That's a cognition as well.

There's also a third one: the thought of making things worse, which probably came from the emotion of fear, or maybe anxiety. "I'm going to make things worse if I say something. If I speak up, it's going to upset my little group here and make things worse."

Underneath that grouping is another group: sensations and impulses. These are consciously accessible, but not nearly as easily as cognitions and emotions. If you're mindfully aware of what's happening within you, you can definitely notice the sensations and the impulses that come along with them.

I think these two reinforce each other. For example, if you have the sensation of heaviness, that heaviness is telling you to immobilize. The impulse would be immobilization. But if you never act on the impulse, the sensation stays there, and we never get to the bottom layer, which is the Polyvagal state. If the impulse is to immobilize, the state is likely shutdown. If you don't listen to the impulse to immobilize, the shutdown never alleviates.

So what sensations did you notice? The obvious ones are her chest tightening and her stomach churning. These might actually come from different Polyvagal states. I think they do, and it might indicate some [Polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) climbing happening for her in real time. I'll come back to that with the Polyvagal state. Other sensations are the heaviness in her limbs and her heart starting to race.
What impulses came along with those sensations?

ul: To speak up. She had the impulse to speak up and just ask questions. It didn't seem like a domineering, dysregulated speaking up. To me it felt more like a powerful speaking up: using her voice and listening to what she needed in that moment, which was clarity from her friends. Within that was an impulse to connect, because she wanted to be a part of it. The impulse to connect, combined with flight or fight activation, results in what I call power, or empowerment. Again, it's not a domineering thing. It's a connective flight or fight kind of thing.
To leave. She wanted to turn off her phone and retreat into her room, to escape. A little bit of flight activation, perhaps.

To hesitate. This one is more subtle. The hesitation is an impulse to immobilize. It's like a little freeze impulse: not to be seen, not to make things worse, to just pause or freeze for a moment until the danger passes.

blocks.p: The last thing is which Polyvagal state or states you see active. I think there are actually a bunch. She seems to be all over the place on the Polyvagal ladder.

Coming home. Let's start at the beginning. She just got off work, and it says she was finally sitting down to relax. The way I read that, work is stressful and overwhelming. I'm just making up a story here, but in my mind she's a nurse who works in the ER. There are sounds going off, there are crises, there's bureaucracy, there are doctors who think they know everything. All of that is overwhelming for her system.

Stress and overwhelm, to me, come from freeze. So she probably comes home in some level of freeze, and she needs to listen to that. She needs to immobilize and decompress. What she should do is actually relax and mindfully let herself decompress: mindfully collapse on the couch and just breathe. Instead, she gets her phone out, and kind of solidifies the freeze.

Can you decompress while watching TV or being on your phone? Yeah, kind of. But if you take that away and just have the present moment, silence, especially if you work in a place like an ER, and you truly collapse when you get home, that's probably a much better recovery. Getting her phone out is not bad, but it's less than ideal.

The trigger. Then she was triggered further into overwhelm, stress, a little bit of freeze, because she felt rejected by her friends. Did her friends intend that? We have no idea. Probably not. But regardless, it tapped into some feeling of rejection within her.

Her chest tightened and her stomach churned. To me, the chest tightening could be evidence of sympathetic activation, and the stomach churning could be evidence of shutdown, which follows the Polyvagal ladder sequentially. It makes sense. These could also be happening at the same time, and maybe there's some freeze activation going on, which I think would definitely be felt in the stomach and in the chest as well.

Plus there was the thought of rejection, which is very disconnected, very away from the group, so lacking safety. In this small moment she has some dysregulation. Not intensely, but at least in this little micro moment, it's there. Personally, I'd say it's more of a freeze, with little access to safety, at least in this small moment.

Racing heart, heavy limbs. Then her heart starts to race and she feels a heaviness in her limbs. In shutdown, does the heart start to race? No, not so much. In freeze? Yeah. In flight or fight? Yeah. But there's also the heaviness in her limbs, which to me suggests some shutdown. Those two together, flight or fight plus shutdown: that's freeze.

She's staring at her phone, so she's immobilized. She's tempted, but she's also hesitating. Again, that indicates freeze to me. Thoughts of making things worse indicate shutdown or freeze, but this keeps pointing me back to freeze.

Pull away, or react. A part of her wants to pull away entirely, to shut off her phone and retreat into her room. That sounds like flight activation. Another part wants to react and demand an explanation, which would probably come more from fight. I don't think it's dysregulated fight, although it actually could be at this point. Retreating to a room and hiding, demanding an explanation: there's not much safety there. So she's probably less in freeze here, and more in flight or fight. That's totally possible. Just because you access freeze in a moment doesn't mean you stay there. It might be a momentary access to freeze, and then the shutdown comes off, and you're left with just flight or fight.

The long breath. What happens next is that she lets out a long breath, not knowing what to do next, indecisive, feeling loneliness and rejection. All of that suggests shutdown to me. Not freeze, but shutdown.

The sequence. So it's possible she came home already in freeze because of overwhelm and stress, and didn't give herself the decompression she needed. Then the overwhelm and stress were reinforced, and she had less and less access to safety. But the freeze wasn't so intense that it became a full-on panic attack and she stayed in freeze. The shutdown may have come off, leaving her with flight or fight. She can't run away from the problem and can't fight it off, so she goes into shutdown at the end.

I could see that being the sequence of events. And these things are rapid. It's not always obvious what state someone is in, and someone's state doesn't always last 30 minutes, or an hour, or all day. It could. There could be a dominant state that flavors the system. Someone could be in shutdown more often than not, but that doesn't mean they're in a chronic 10 out of 10 shutdown all day. At one point it might be a 10. At another point it might be a two, with more access to safety, or more access to flight or fight.

So for Maria, we might be looking at really rapid shifts in Polyvagal state that follow the sequence. It's also possible this was written by AI, and the AI is confused and doesn't understand the sequence of autonomic ladder shifts.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: I know it's not always easy to recognize what's happening within you: your emotions, your cognitions, your sensations, your impulses, and even your Polyvagal state. If you can practice acknowledging these domains in a story, maybe it becomes easier to do it for yourself, truthfully. Good luck in your own validation.
